word_order: SVO — subjects precede verbs and objects follow them in sentences like 'Steve Jobs unveiled the device' and 'Mutations can have a variety of different effects.'
register: Formal, edited written expository prose (encyclopedic/news-style factual sentences).
fillers_and_hesitations: minimal hesitation particles (um, uh) — not attested in this written sample
discourse_markers: commentary/adverbial discourse markers that frame claims (of course, in the end)
temporal connectives that introduce adverbial clauses or phrases (after, once)
clause_boundary_signals: subordinating conjunctions and complementizers that introduce subordinate clauses (although, because)
relative pronouns introducing relative clauses (that, which)
coordinating conjunctions that conjoin independent clauses (and, but)
auxiliary and finite verb forms that realize clause tense/aspect and typically occupy clause-final morphology in subordinate sequences (was, have)
non_boundary_traps: nominal 'of' prepositional phrases inside NPs that look like separate units but are internal (of the Apollo X command module)
titles and name sequences or appositive name phrases that superficially resemble clauses (Sir, CEO)
short parenthetical modifiers or descriptors that appear clause-like but modify a noun (live on television; the bank’s nationalisation)
unstable_prefix_signals: fronted adverbial/subordinate elements whose attachment remains open until the main verb appears (while visiting, after the war)
prepositional or temporal phrases at the clause start that do not fix predicate structure (because of, once)
notes_for_prompt_writer: This sample is standard edited English (SVO) with frequent fronted adverbial/subordinate material and multiword named entities. Relative clauses use that/which/who and subordinators like although/because commonly introduce embedded propositions. Many noun phrases contain internal 'of' prepositional phrases and titles that should be treated as nominal material rather than independent clauses. Participial/‑ing fronted phrases (e.g., 'while visiting') can create attachment ambiguity until the main verb or subject appears.
